title: Invalid cursor values can escape the tool-level error handling
reasoning: mail_fetch expects cursor decoding failures to be converted into a structured MailFetchResult error, but _decode_cursor_value only catches ValueError, JSONDecodeError, and UnicodeDecodeError. base64 decoding can also raise binascii.Error for malformed padding, and cursor.encode('ascii') can raise UnicodeEncodeError for non-ASCII cursor strings. Those exceptions bypass the ValueError handler in mail_fetch and can fail the whole MCP request instead of returning a normal tool error.
reproduction: Call mail_fetch with cursor='abc' to trigger incorrect base64 padding, or with a non-ASCII cursor string to trigger UnicodeEncodeError before the JSON parsing path.
recommendation: Catch binascii.Error and UnicodeEncodeError in _decode_cursor_value and re-raise ValueError('Invalid cursor payload') so all malformed cursors follow the existing structured error path.
whyTestsDoNotAlreadyCoverThis: No linked tests were included for malformed cursor handling; the shown code only demonstrates the intended ValueError recovery path.
suggestedRegressionTest: Add a mail_fetch test that passes cursor='abc' and another non-ASCII cursor, asserting the response contains an errors entry instead of raising.
minimumFixScope: Update _decode_cursor_value exception handling and add focused cursor validation tests.

history.reasoning: The current /workspace/src/imap_readonly_mcp/server.py still contains the relevant code, but _decode_cursor_value now imports binascii and catches both UnicodeEncodeError and binascii.Error along with the prior JSON/Unicode/value errors, then re-raises ValueError("Invalid cursor payload"). mail_fetch still catches ValueError from _merge_cursor and returns a structured MailFetchResult with an errors entry, so malformed base64 cursors like 'abc' and non-ASCII cursors should no longer escape tool-level error handling.
